title: 2 Kings 4:1–7
context: Chapter 4 turns from international war to the needs of ordinary households, presenting a series of Elisha’s miracles. The first concerns the widow of one of the sons of the prophets, a community of prophets associated with Elisha. A creditor is about to take her two children as slaves to settle a debt, a practice the law sought to limit and regulate (Leviticus 25:39–43). Elisha directs her to gather empty containers, and a single pot of oil fills them all until none remain; she sells the oil, pays the debt, and lives on the rest with her sons. Both traditions read the story as a display of the LORD’s care for the widow and the fatherless, carried out through simple, trusting obedience.

verses.text: Now a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets cried out to Elisha, saying, “Your servant my husband is dead. You know that your servant feared the LORD. Now the creditor has come to take for himself my two children to be slaves.”
verses.arminianNotes: A widow of one of the sons of the prophets cries out to Elisha because her husband, who feared the LORD, has died, and a creditor threatens to take her two children as slaves. Arminian readers note that faithfulness does not exempt believers from loss and hardship, and that her honest cry is itself an act of trust in God’s servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the LORD who defends the widow and the fatherless (Deuteronomy 10:18; Psalm 68:5) is not indifferent to the family of one who feared him. Both traditions agree that the verse exposes the vulnerability of widows and children in ancient Israel, which the law sought to restrain (Leviticus 25:39–43), and that God’s care reaches into economic need.

verses.text: Elisha said to her, “What should I do for you? Tell me, what do you have in the house?” She said, “Your servant has nothing in the house, except a pot of oil.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha asks what she wants and what she has in the house, and she has only a pot of oil. Arminian readers see the prophet engaging her as a participant, inviting her to bring what little she has, so that the provision to come begins with her own cooperation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that God often begins with what seems insufficient so that the abundance that follows is clearly his gift. Both traditions agree that the small pot of oil becomes the means of provision, and that Elisha’s question honors the woman’s agency while directing her toward the LORD’s help.

verses.text: Then he said, “Go, borrow empty containers from all your neighbors. Don’t borrow just a few containers.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha tells her to borrow many empty containers from her neighbors, not just a few. Arminian readers note that the measure of her obedience will shape the measure of what she receives, and they see an invitation to expectant faith that acts boldly on God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the command God’s generosity, which invites more than human imagination would think to ask. Both traditions agree that the neighbors’ containers draw the wider community into the story, and that the instruction calls for trust before any miracle is visible.

verses.text: Go in and shut the door on you and on your sons, and pour oil into all those containers; and set aside those which are full.”
verses.arminianNotes: She is told to shut the door on herself and her sons and pour oil into the containers. Arminian readers note the private, family-centered setting of the miracle, where the widow and her sons act together in obedience to the prophet’s instruction, sharing in what God is about to do.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the shut door keeps attention on the LORD’s quiet provision rather than on public display or on the prophet himself. Both traditions agree that the instructions are specific and practical, and that the widow’s obedience is the setting in which God’s provision unfolds.

verses.text: So she went from him, and shut the door on herself and on her sons. They brought the containers to her, and she poured oil.
verses.arminianNotes: The widow obeys, shutting the door while her sons bring containers and she pours. Arminian readers highlight her immediate obedience and the cooperation of her children, showing faith expressed through ordinary action in response to God’s word spoken through his prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her obedience as the fruit of faith that God himself sustains, and the work of the household as the setting of his provision. Both traditions agree that the family’s simple, trusting labor is the pattern the narrator commends, and that the miracle happens in the midst of that labor.

verses.text: When the containers were full, she said to her son, “Bring me another container.” He said to her, “There isn’t another container.” Then the oil stopped flowing.
verses.arminianNotes: The oil flows until there is no other container, and then it stops. Arminian readers often note that the supply matched the vessels gathered, suggesting that the scope of her expectant obedience corresponded to the scope of what she received from God’s hand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the oil stops exactly when the LORD’s purpose is complete, showing his precise and sufficient provision. Both traditions agree that the miracle supplies abundantly and that the stopping of the oil points beyond the jars to the One who controls the flow.

verses.text: Then she came and told the man of God. He said, “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt; and you and your sons live on the rest.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha tells her to sell the oil, pay her debt, and live on the rest with her sons. Arminian readers note that God’s provision restores her family’s freedom and secures its future, and that the man of God directs her to honest repayment of what she owes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in this a display of God’s faithful care, delivering the children from slavery and the widow from want. Both traditions agree that the story shows God’s concern for justice, family, and daily bread, and that his provision covers both the debt and the life that follows.
